input.question: How can there be a maximum speed if there is no absolute frame of reference in space?
input.ground_truth: > I could travel at a constant speed, choose myself as the frame of reference and claim that I'm standing still. Now, suppose I first accelerate to the speed of 0.99c, then establish my current fixed speed as the speed 0. Wouldn't I then be able to continue to accelerate, eventually past c? Yes. You can. The difference however is that, in relation to an observer "standing still", time is passing slower for you, your length is contracted etc. So, in relation to this observer you won't be able to reach *c*. However, in your perspective, you really will be able to reach your destination faster if you keep accelerating as if relativity didn't exist. The thing is that you will reach your destination faster because as you accelerate, time slows down for you, so in a blink of an eye, you're in the other side of the universe (depending on how much you accelerated from 0.99c)

Question: How can there be a maximum speed if there is no absolute frame of reference in space?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you and your friend are both on skateboards, floating in space where there’s no ground or walls. You both start rolling in different directions. If you look at your friend while you’re moving, it might look like they’re moving really fast away from you. But if your friend looks at you, it looks like you’re moving really fast away from them!

Now, scientists found out that nothing can go faster than light—like a super-fast laser beam. This is called the “speed of light limit.” But you might wonder, “If there’s no ‘standing still’ spot in space, how do we know what’s fast or slow?”

Well, here’s the thing: even though there’s no special ‘standing still’ spot, everyone in space can agree on how fast light moves. No matter how fast you or your friend are moving, you both will always see light zipping by at the same super-fast speed. Because of that, scientists can say, “Nothing can go faster than light!” That’s the “maximum speed” rule.

So, even without a special ‘rest’ spot, everyone can still agree on how fast light goes, and that helps us know what the fastest possible speed is.
